summary: This document clarifies how the Local Protection Desired bit is used in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP). It also adds a new flag for signaling that protection must be enforced. It updates RFC 5440.

plainLanguage.summary: A map helper can be asked for a route with a backup road. This makes the request clearer and adds a way to say "the backup road is a must, not a maybe."

questions: what is the pcep e flag
what does the local protection desired bit do
subtitle: A new E flag lets a PCEP request say whether path protection is a must or only a preference.

tldr.problem: The Local Protection Desired (L) flag in PCEP is a single bit, and implementations read it as either mandatory or preferred protection, so behavior differed.
tldr.mechanism: A new Protection Enforcement (E) flag in the LSPA object, combined with the L flag, selects one of four constraints: protection mandatory, unprotected mandatory, protection preferred or unprotected preferred.
tldr.outcome: Operators can state exactly how strict the PCE must be, and the PCE behaves consistently across implementations. Peers that do not know the E flag ignore it.

today: RFC 9488 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2023. It updates RFC 5440 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) ask a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute paths. The Local Protection Desired (L) flag in the LSPA object comes from RSVP-TE (RFC 3209), where it tells downstream routers they may use a local repair mechanism. The headend does not know whether a downstream router will protect a hop, so in RSVP the L flag does not force transit routers to provide protection.

With Segment Routing (RFC 8664), each SID may offer local protection, and a PCE can learn this through BGP-LS and use it as a path constraint. Operators want to control how strictly that requirement is enforced. This document updates RFC 5440 by clarifying the L flag and adding the Protection Enforcement (E) flag. The text uses Segment Routing as context but is agnostic about path setup type and data plane.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for a route, you can say you would like a backup road. This document makes that request clearer and lets you say how much you care.

sections.title: Why One Bit Was Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 5440 says that when the L flag is set, the computed path must include links protected with Fast Reroute. But the flag is named 'Desired', and implementations have read it as either PROTECTION MANDATORY or PROTECTION PREFERRED, leading to operational differences.

A single boolean also cannot tell apart the four options an operator may want, which usually follow from a Service Level Agreement. Protection mandatory suits an LSP that must be fast rerouted on any failure. Unprotected mandatory suits an LSP that is already protected by a secondary diverse LSP. There, local protection could push traffic over links that break TE requirements such as bandwidth, or lead to the LSP being torn down anyway, so it is better to tear it down at once and use the established secondary path.

The two PREFERRED options relax the constraint. Protection status does not cause links to be pruned, but it gives the PCE a priority when choosing. With Segment Routing, an adjacency may have both a protected and an unprotected SID. UNPROTECTED PREFERRED picks the unprotected SID and PROTECTED PREFERRED picks the protected one.
sections.plainLanguage: Saying 'I want a backup road' with a simple yes or no is not enough. Sometimes you insist on one, sometimes you would rather not have one, and sometimes you just lean one way.

sections.title: The Four Protection Constraints
sections.content:
The document defines four terms for how protection eligibility applies to the links of a path:

  • PROTECTION MANDATORY: the path MUST have protection eligibility on all links.
  • UNPROTECTED MANDATORY: the path MUST NOT have protection eligibility on all links.
  • PROTECTION PREFERRED: the path should have protection eligibility on all links but might contain links that do not.
  • UNPROTECTED PREFERRED: the path should not have protection eligibility on all links but might contain links that do.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways to ask: 'backup road required', 'no backup road allowed', 'backup road if possible' and 'no backup road if possible'.

sections.title: The E Flag in the LSPA Object
sections.content:
The E (Protection Enforcement) flag is bit 6 of the 8-bit Flags field in the LSPA object. The L flag stays at bit 7. The L flag says whether protection is desired (1) or not (0). The E flag controls how strictly the PCE must apply it. When E is 1, the value of L needs to be respected during resource selection. When E is 0, the PCE tries to respect L but could relax or ignore it.

The combinations are:

  • L=1, E=1: the PCE MUST treat it as PROTECTION MANDATORY.
  • L=1, E=0: the PCE MUST treat it as PROTECTION PREFERRED.
  • L=0, E=0: the PCE SHOULD treat it as UNPROTECTED PREFERRED, but MAY treat it as UNPROTECTED MANDATORY, for example if it can detect a legacy PCC that expects the old behavior.
  • L=0, E=1: the PCE MUST treat it as UNPROTECTED MANDATORY.

If the PCE cannot infer the protection status of a resource, it MAY use local policy. For Segment Routing paths it is RECOMMENDED to assume a Node SID is protected, and an Adjacency SID is protected if its backup flag is set.
sections.plainLanguage: The L switch says 'I would like a backup road'. The E switch says 'and I really mean it'. Together they give four different answers.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
A PCC or PCE that does not support this document ignores the E flag and sets it to 0 in PCRpt and PCUpd messages. A PCE that does not support it sends PCUpd with E set to 0 for PCC-initiated LSPs even if the earlier message had 1, and a PCC that does not support it sends PCRpt with E set to 0 for PCE-initiated LSPs.

A supporting PCC MAY set E to 1 depending on local configuration. If its PCE does not support the document, the PCE follows RFC 5440 and ignores E, so the computed path might not respect the enforcement constraint.

For PCC-initiated LSPs, the PCC SHOULD ignore the E flag received in a PCUpd message. For PCE-initiated LSPs, the PCC MAY process it, and the PCE SHOULD ignore the E flag received in a PCRpt message.
sections.plainLanguage: If one side has not heard of the new switch, it simply pretends the switch is off. So old and new equipment can still talk, but the 'really mean it' part may not be honored.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The document clarifies an existing flag and adds a new one that gives more control over it. It creates no new sensitive information and says no additional security measure is required. Securing the PCEP session with TLS (RFC 8253), following the best current practices in RFC 9325, is RECOMMENDED.

IANA allocated bit 6, Protection Enforcement, in the LSPA Object Flag Field subregistry of the PCEP Numbers registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The new switch does not reveal any secrets. It is still wise to keep the conversation private.
